``` ::: ::: `PyFixest` specifies different regression models by Wilkinson Formulas via the `formulaic` package. Wilkinson formulas should be familiar to you if you have used R's `lm()` or `statsmodels` formula API. Many additional ideas implemented in `PyFixest` have been developed in the `fixest` package (most notably multiple estimation syntax, the i-operator, sample splitting). By default, all formula options presented here are supported by all models available via the `pf.feols()`, `pf.feglm()`, and `pf.fepois()` APIs. ## Basic Syntax In the simplest case, we regress covariates `X1` and `X2` on `Y`. ::: {#32657ad5 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit1 = pf.feols("Y ~ X1 + X2", data=data) fit1.summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ### Estimation: OLS Dep. var.: Y sample: None = all Inference: iid Observations: 998 | Coefficient | Estimate | Std. Error | t value | Pr(>|t|) | 2.5% | 97.5% | |:--------------|-----------:|-------------:|----------:|-----------:|-------:|--------:| | Intercept | 0.889 | 0.108 | 8.197 | 0.000 | 0.676 | 1.102 | | X1 | -0.993 | 0.082 | -12.092 | 0.000 | -1.154 | -0.832 | | X2 | -0.176 | 0.022 | -8.102 | 0.000 | -0.219 | -0.134 | --- RMSE: 2.09 R2: 0.177 ``` ::: ::: In the covariate part of the formula, transformations supported by `formulaic` are also supported by `PyFixest`. To name just a few important ones, you can create categorical variables via the `C()` operator: ::: {#823885ee .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit2 = pf.feols("Y ~ X1 + X2 + C(f1)", data=data) ``` ::: You can interact variables via the `*` and `:` operators: ::: {#a43fc270 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit3 = pf.feols("Y ~ X1:X2", data=data) fit4 = pf.feols("Y ~ X1*X2", data=data) pf.etable([fit3, fit4]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: To create logarithms of a function, just use ::: {#8902c173 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit5 = pf.feols("Y ~ log(X1)", data=data) ``` ::: or use any `numpy` transforms, e.g. ::: {#3c09311a .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit5 = pf.feols("Y ~ X1 + np.power(X1,2)", data=data) ``` ::: Note - for the logarithm, we suggest to not rely on `np.log` but use the internal `log` operator. ## Fixed Effects Syntax We can add fixed effects behind the `|` operator: here we add two fixed effects `f1` and `f2`. ::: {#00286095 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit6 = pf.feols("Y ~ X1 + X2 | f1 + f2", data=data) ``` ::: We can interact two fixed effects via the `:` operator. If you are coming from `fixest`, note that its `^` operator is deprecated here: see [Deprecated spellings](#deprecated-spellings). ::: {#42911185 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit7 = pf.feols("Y ~ X1 + X2 | f1:f2", data=data) ``` ::: For details on fixed effects regression, take a look at the [OLS with Fixed Effects](ols-fixed-effects.qmd) vignette. Fixed effects must be data columns or interactions of data columns. Their names must be valid Python identifiers, cannot be Python keywords, and must use Python's normalized identifier spelling. Rename FE columns containing spaces or punctuation before estimation. FE transforms such as `I(f1 + f2)` and `C(f1)` are unsupported; create the transformed column in `data` first. Outcome, covariate, and instrument names can still be quoted with backticks, for example ``"Y ~ `my covariate` | firm"``. ### Varying slopes Use `f1[X2]` to let the slope on `X2` vary across levels of `f1`, or `f1[[X2]]` to include only the slopes. Separate several slopes with commas, as in `f1[X2, Z1]`. Slopes also work with interacted groups (`f1:f2[X2]`) and arithmetic expressions (`f1[X2**2]`). ::: {#b64dff32 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit_slopes = pf.feols("Y ~ X1 | f1[X2] + f2", data=data) fit_slopes_only = pf.feols("Y ~ X1 | f1[[X2, Z1]]", data=data) pf.etable([fit_slopes, fit_slopes_only]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Varying slopes work with `feols()`, including IV, `fepois()`, and `feglm()`, and require the default `within` demeaner. `predict()`, `fixef()`, `wildboottest()`, `ritest()`, `decompose()`, and CRV3 or HAC inference are not yet supported for these models. Slope-only effects such as `f1[[X2]]` do not absorb the constant, so the model keeps and reports an `Intercept`. Effects with level-specific intercepts, such as `f1[X2]`, absorb it. Write `0 +` on the right-hand side to drop the intercept of a slope-only model: ::: {#e40263be .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} pf.feols("Y ~ X1 | f1[[X2]]", data=data).coef() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` Coefficient Intercept 0.874957 X1 -0.991049 Name: Estimate, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ## Instrumental Variables (IV) Syntax For IV estimation, `PyFixest` 0.70 uses Formulaic's bracketed multistage syntax. The endogenous variable and its instruments go in a square-bracket block on the right-hand side. Fixed effects stay behind the `|`, exactly as in a model without instruments: ```python "Y ~ exogenous_controls + [endogenous ~ instruments] | fixed_effects" ``` Here is a minimal example with fixed effects: ::: {#d7314309 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit_iv = pf.feols("Y ~ X2 + [X1 ~ Z1] | f1 + f2", data=data) fit_iv.summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ### Estimation: IV Dep. var.: Y, Fixed effects: f1+f2 sample: None = all Inference: iid Observations: 997 | Coefficient | Estimate | Std. Error | t value | Pr(>|t|) | 2.5% | 97.5% | |:--------------|-----------:|-------------:|----------:|-----------:|-------:|--------:| | X2 | -0.174 | 0.015 | -11.701 | 0.000 | -0.204 | -0.145 | | X1 | -1.050 | 0.089 | -11.793 | 0.000 | -1.225 | -0.875 | --- ``` ::: ::: The main formula decides whether both stages have an intercept: `Y ~ 0 + [X1 ~ Z1]` omits it from the first and second stage. A `0`, `-1` or `1` inside the brackets has no effect. Before version `0.70.0`, `PyFixest` supported instrumental variables syntax similar to `fixest`'s. For example, the IV model above would have been written as `Y ~ X2 | f1 + f2 | X1 ~ Z1`. This syntax is deprecated: it raises a `DeprecationWarning` in 0.70 and will become an error in a future release. See the [formula-parsing changelog](/changelog.qmd#formula-parsing-on-formulaic) for details. For all the details on IV estimation, take a look at the [Instrumental Variables](instrumental-variables.qmd) vignette. ## The `i()` operator for interacting fixed effects For interacting fixed effects, we include a specialised operator `i()` If you simply wrap a variable into `i()`, it will be treated just as the `C()` operator (see above). ::: {#395691aa .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit_i = pf.feols("Y ~ i(f1)", data=data) fit_c = pf.feols("Y ~ C(f1)", data=data) ``` ::: But overall, `i()` is more powerful than `C()`. Most importantly, you can easily set the reference level of the categorical variable: ::: {#d384e140 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # set 1 as reference level fit_i1 = pf.feols("Y ~ i(f1, ref = 1)", data=data) ``` ::: You can also easily interact variables: ::: {#5da8dfa2 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} # set 1 as reference level fit_i2 = pf.feols("Y ~ i(f1, f2)", data=data) ``` ::: A numeric second variable such as `f2` by default enters as a continuous slope. To enforce that it is treated as a categorical, you can Wrap it in `C()`, and set reference levels for both via the `ref` and `ref2` arguments. ::: {#c9bbfaf3 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} # set 1 and 2 as reference levels fit_i3 = pf.feols("Y ~ i(f1, C(f2), ref = 1, ref2 = 2)", data=data) ``` ::: This is in particular useful for difference-in-differences models. Last, you can bin levels of a variable via the `bin` argument. This groups multiple levels into a single category. ::: {#0400306e .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit_bin = pf.feols( "Y ~ i(f1, bin={'low': list(range(0, 10)), 'mid': list(range(10, 20)), 'high': list(range(20, 30))}, ref='low')", data=data, ) fit_bin.summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ### Estimation: OLS Dep. var.: Y sample: None = all Inference: iid Observations: 998 | Coefficient | Estimate | Std. Error | t value | Pr(>|t|) | 2.5% | 97.5% | |:--------------|-----------:|-------------:|----------:|-----------:|-------:|--------:| | Intercept | -0.473 | 0.122 | -3.887 | 0.000 | -0.712 | -0.234 | | f1::high | 0.110 | 0.174 | 0.630 | 0.529 | -0.232 | 0.451 | | f1::mid | 0.968 | 0.176 | 5.503 | 0.000 | 0.623 | 1.313 | --- RMSE: 2.264 R2: 0.035 ``` ::: ::: ## Multiple Estimation Syntax Last, `PyFixest` provides syntactic sugar to fit multiple estimations in one go. This not only economizes on lines-of-code, but also allows for performance optimizations via caching. When several models are fit on the same sample and share the same fixed-effect structure, `PyFixest` can reuse already-demeaned columns across models. For the LSMR demeaner backend, it can also reuse the fixed-effect preconditioner across models with the same structure. If you fit many regression models on a fixed set of fixed effects and many overlapping covariates or dependent variables, and performance is poor, we highly recommend you to try out multiple estimations. For multiple estimations, we provide 5 custom operators: `sw`, `csw`, `sw0`, `csw0` and `mvsw`. Use `sw()` on the left-hand side for multiple dependent variables. ### Multiple dependent variables You can wrap several dependent variables in `sw()`, e.g. via `"sw(Y1, Y2) ~ X1"`, to fit one model per dependent variable. ::: {#20b0e713 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit_multi_dep = pf.feols("sw(Y, Y2) ~ X1 + X2", data=data) pf.etable(fit_multi_dep) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Multiple Estimation, caching and performance The speedup from multiple-estimation syntax is most visible when models have the same fixed effects and overlapping covariates. Below, we therefore benchmark ```text y ~ csw(x1, x2, ..., x16) | indiv_id + firm_id + year ``` to demonstrate the speed gains possible with multiple estimation and caching. In the specified multiple estimation formula, we fit sixteen models via one`csw()` call. Those sixteen models fit can be sped up by caching already demeaned variables. The idea is very simple - after the first fit, `y` and `x1` are already demeaned, so we do not have to do it again in fit 2. After fit 2, `x2` is demeaned, so we do not need to do it again in fit 3, and so on. In contrast, if you fit the sixteen models one by one, you have to demean `y` and `x1` in all 16 specifications and set up the preconditioner for every fit. How much faster could the caching of already-demeaned variables potentially make the estimation? For simplicity, let's assume that the demeaning step takes 100% of the runtime of a call to `pf.feols()`, and that the runtime of demeaning scales perfectly linearly in the number of columns that are demeaned. In the 16 separate regression fits, in total we would have to demean `y` and `x1` 16 times, `x2` 15 times, ..., and `x16` once. So in total, we would have to demean `16 + 16 + 15 + 14 + ... + 1 = 152` columns across the sixteen separate fits. In contrast, in the multiple-estimation path, we only have to demean each of the 17 unique columns (`y`, `x1`, ..., `x16`) once. If demeaning were 100% of the algorithm runtime and scaled perfectly linearly in the number of columns, the upper bound on the speedup from caching already-demeaned variables would be `152 / 17 = 8.9x`. In practice, the realized speedup is lower because each model still pays for formula and model-matrix construction, sample handling, fitting the OLS model, inference, and post-processing. Note that in addition to caching already-demeaned variables, all model fits can also share preconditioners. As building a preconditioner can be costly (in particular the "additive" preconditioner), this can lead to large speedups when fitting many models on the same sample with the same fixed effects. To demonstrate realistic speed gains, we compare the multiple-estimation call specified above with fitting the same sixteen formulas one by one using the `fixest` benchmark DGPs described in [When Are Fixed Effects Estimations Difficult?](../explanation/difficult-fixed-effects.md). ::: {#cd0ece9e .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show benchmark code"} import time import sys from pathlib import Path import pandas as pd repo_root = next( path for path in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents] if (path / "benchmarks/modular/dgp_functions.py").exists() ) sys.path.insert(0, str(repo_root)) from benchmarks.modular.dgp_functions import base_dgp model_k = 16 rhs_terms = [f"x{i}" for i in range(1, model_k + 1)] multi_formula = ( f"y ~ csw({', '.join(rhs_terms)}) | indiv_id + firm_id + year" ) single_formulas = [ f"y ~ {' + '.join(f'x{j}' for j in range(1, i + 1))} | indiv_id + firm_id + year" for i in range(1, model_k + 1) ] demeaners = { "MAP (rust)": pf.MapDemeaner(backend="rust"), "LSMR diagonal": pf.LsmrDemeaner( backend="within", preconditioner="diagonal", fixef_maxiter=10_000, ), "LSMR additive": pf.LsmrDemeaner( backend="within", preconditioner="additive", fixef_maxiter=10_000, ), } def _time_once(fn): start = time.perf_counter() fn() return time.perf_counter() - start rows = [] for dgp_name in ["simple", "difficult"]: bench_data = base_dgp( n=100_000, type_=dgp_name, k=model_k, max_k=model_k, seed=929, ) for demeaner_name, demeaner in demeaners.items(): pf.feols(single_formulas[0], data=bench_data, demeaner=demeaner, lean=True) multi_seconds = _time_once( lambda: pf.feols( multi_formula, data=bench_data, demeaner=demeaner, lean=True, ) ) separate_seconds = _time_once( lambda: [ pf.feols(fml, data=bench_data, demeaner=demeaner, lean=True) for fml in single_formulas ] ) rows.append( { "DGP": dgp_name, "Demeaner": demeaner_name, "Separate fits (s)": separate_seconds, "Multiple estimation (s)": multi_seconds, "Speedup": separate_seconds / multi_seconds, } ) ( pd.DataFrame(rows) .assign( **{ "Separate fits (s)": lambda x: x["Separate fits (s)"].round(3), "Multiple estimation (s)": lambda x: x["Multiple estimation (s)"].round(3), "Speedup": lambda x: x["Speedup"].map(lambda value: f"{value:.2f}x"), } ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Deprecated spellings We are deprecating multiple `fixest`-style syntax features with `PyFixest` 0.70.0. Our stated goal is to "mimic fixest syntax as much as Python allows". Most of the changes below stem from the fact that our model matrix engine `formulaic` supports the novel syntax better / easier, which leads to cleaner and less buggy code. | Deprecated | Use instead | |---|---| | `Y ~ X1 | f1^f2` | `Y ~ X1 | f1:f2` | | `Y ~ X1 | f1 | X2 ~ Z1` | `Y ~ X1 + [X2 ~ Z1] | f1` | | `Y + Y2 ~ X1` | `sw(Y, Y2) ~ X1` | The instrument block moves onto the right-hand side, so an IV model without fixed effects reads `Y ~ X1 + [X2 ~ Z1]`. The `|` separator is now reserved for fixed effects. ## Where to Go Next - [OLS with Fixed Effects](ols-fixed-effects.qmd): practical FE estimation patterns. - [Difference-in-Differences](difference-in-differences.qmd): event-study applications with `i()`. - [Regression Tables](regression-tables.qmd): organize and export many-model workflows. - [How-To: Translating Stata to PyFixest](../how-to/stata-2-pyfixest.qmd): syntax mapping and defaults.
